script.opening_words: You just got promoted. Congratulations. Your salary jumped from 38,000 to $50,000 a year. And for about three weeks, you felt like you were finally making it. You updated your LinkedIn, maybe treated yourself to dinner at that restaurant you always walk past but never enter, and started thinking about all the things you could finally afford. Fast forward 6 months, and somehow you're more stressed about money than you were before the raise. Your bank account looks eerily similar
script.ending_words: the math itself. You're not failing at budgeting. You're succeeding at surviving in a system designed to keep you running in place while convincing you that the treadmill is actually a path to somewhere better. The real mirage isn't just the money. It's the promise that working harder and earning more will eventually set you free. When the game is rigged to expand your expenses faster than your income can
script.analysis: Full 19206 canonical characters read. Hook: a $38K to $50K promotion that feels like broke within six months, framed as the "paycheck mirage". One budget sketch ($50K to ~$38K take-home, ~$3,000/month; $1,500 rent; $400 car; ~$800 left) whose arithmetic roughly reproduces, with a low implied insurance-and-utilities total. The rest is an essay on lifestyle inflation, credit availability, social comparison, the advice industry, subscriptions, dating, student loans, a $3,000 deductible (above the KFF $1,886 average), the 15% retirement rule ($7,500 reproduces) and family-wealth gaps. Few sourced statistics; most claims are illustrative or opinion. The stored text ends mid-sentence, so the closing may be missing from the stored caption.
